WHAT YOU'RE SEEING

Reliability is a spending limit.

Think of an error budget as pocket money for failures. Your experiment gets only part of that money. The controller tries to learn about weaknesses while keeping enough money in reserve to stop safely.

A fire drill for your application.

THE WHOLE CEP IN ONE SENTENCE

“How hard can we test the app before we spend our allowance for failures?”

The controller is the person watching the allowance. Attribution is checking which failures the test actually caused. The watchdog is a separate person who stops the drill if the controller disappears.

Four modules, one feedback loop

→→→

The first three inform the live loop. The oracle summarizes completed runs; it does not predict the future.

Where the real tools fit

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

What this visualizer simplifies

It samples synthetic requests using a fixed seed, with no shared infrastructure, retries, or delayed telemetry. Intentional delays are 600ms; requests over 500ms or failed requests count against the latency SLO. Healthy responses have no extra random latency.

The allocation is frozen at admission from a declared 120-second reservation, even when traffic changes. We do not observe that entire horizon. The loop uses instantaneous synthetic observations; its reserve does not simulate real cleanup damage. Known background failures cancel only approximately because cohorts have different random samples.

The normal teaching mode charges the nonnegative point estimate of extra failures. The optional repository mode uses the same per-interval Wilson formula as the Python code. Neither mode validates the real controller, proves causality, or establishes a strict budget bound.

SAME PROBLEM. FOUR APPROACHES.

Who spends the budget better?

Run all four policies with matched synthetic traffic and the sandbox's current settings. Look at both damage and useful testing: stopping immediately is safe, but teaches very little.

Same seed · same allocation · same emergency guards
▥

Four controllers. One shared starting point.

Press “Run fair comparison” to explore the tradeoff.

Read these results carefully

These are 60-second teaching simulations using one seed, not the CEP's final empirical evaluation. The preplanned policy uses an illustrative cost of one bad request per affected request. It has not been calibrated on cluster pilots. Adaptive behavior is inspired by the prototype; time windows and real actuator delays are simplified.

All policies share an emergency allocation guard. Similar overshoot can mean the shared guard dominated the comparison. No winner is claimed from this demonstration.
